name: Impossible Burger (Composite)
notes:
Impossible Burger modelled from its ingredients (a composite). A separate 'Impossible Meat' entry built from Impossible Foods' own Quantis LCA was removed on 2026-10-01 to avoid listing the same product twice; the Quantis LCA is still used here for factory emissions.

The recipe is worked out from the 2023 label: ~22% soy protein concentrate, ~5.5% each sunflower and coconut oil (solved from total and saturated fat), ~5% minor ingredients, ~62% water. Soy protein concentrate is traced back to soybeans. Crop impacts (land, water, pesticides, farm emissions) come from those ingredients' own entries. Factory emissions (~2.3 kg CO2e/kg) come from the Quantis LCA, including heme fermentation, and are added on top.

Availability blends the product's own volume (~2.7 Gg/yr, from the 2018 Oakland plant) with its ingredients' world supply, so it isn't penalised for being a small brand. The recipe shares are confidence 2: labels only give ingredient order, not amounts.

Vitamins and minerals not on the label are a rough guess from its ingredients' values and recipe shares.

source.note: Impossible Meat — nutrition: FDC 2664240 (Impossible Foods label, 2023 recipe) per 100 g raw: 204 kcal, fat 11.5 g, sat fat 5.31 g, protein 16.81 g, fiber 4.4 g, sodium 327 mg, carbs 7.96 g, sugars 0.88 g, cholesterol 0, trans fat 0; converted to per gram. source.note: Impossible Burger — kg soybeans charged per kg SPC: ~1.7 kg beans make 1 kg SPC by mass (0.79 kg meal per kg beans x ~0.75 SPC yield from meal), but the beans also yield ~0.19 kg oil. With economic allocation (meal carries ~60% of the bean's impact, as in the soy entry's farm-gate note) that is ~0.76 kg bean-equivalent per kg meal / 0.75 -> ~1.0 per kg SPC. Cross-check: Quantis gives soy protein ~24% of 2.5 m2·yr/kg = 0.6 m2 per kg burger, i.e. ~0.2 kg beans at US yields, same as 0.22 x 1.0.

source.note: Impossible Burger — processing emissions: Quantis Table 15 total 3.50 kg CO2e/kg = ingredients 2.09 + production 1.38 + packaging 0.02. name: Beyond Burger (Composite)
notes:
Beyond Burger modelled from its ingredients (a composite). The recipe is worked out from the label: ~19% pea protein, ~7% canola oil, ~4% coconut oil, ~3% rice protein, ~7% minor ingredients (flavours, yeast, cocoa butter, methylcellulose), ~60% water. The oil shares are solved from total and saturated fat; rice protein is a rough estimate (confidence 1).

Crop impacts come from the ingredients' entries: pea protein traces back to peas, rice protein to rice. Factory, packaging, cold storage and ingredient transport emissions (~1.7 kg CO2e/kg) come from the Heller & Keoleian 2018 University of Michigan LCA.

Availability blends Beyond Meat's 2024 sales volume (31.8 Gg, all products, so it overstates the burger) with its ingredients' supply.

Vitamins and minerals not on the label are a rough guess from its ingredients' values and recipe shares.

name: Violife Just Like Parmesan (Composite)
notes:
Violife's vegan Parmesan-style wedge, modelled from its ingredients. The recipe comes from the US label: ~17.5% coconut oil, ~28% potato starch, ~6% rice starch, ~3% rice protein, ~3.5% salt, ~40% water. Coconut oil and potato starch are the main crop impacts.

The non-crop part (manufacturing, packaging, distribution, retail) is 2.1 kg CO2e/kg. That's Quantis' 2022 LCA total for this product (3.4) minus the crops modelled here.

Upfield publishes no Violife volumes, so its own availability is a deliberately low guess (0.5 Gg/yr, confidence 1), blended with its ingredients' supply. The nutrition is weak on protein (about 3.6 g per 100 g), which is the main reason it trails dairy Parmesan on nutrition.

Vitamins and minerals not on the label are a rough guess from its ingredients' values and recipe shares.

name: Follow Your Heart Parmesan Grated (Composite)
notes:

name: Coca-Cola (Composite)
notes:
Regular Coca-Cola, modelled from its ingredients: 10.6% sugar by weight (39 g per 355 mL can), split 85% cane / 15% beet like world sugar supply. The rest is carbonated water, caramel colour, phosphoric acid, flavours and caffeine, which have no crop footprint. The US version uses high fructose corn syrup, which isn't modelled.

Nutrition is from Coke's own label. It's pure sugar calories and has the worst nutrition score in the dataset.

Factory, can, distribution, chilling and disposal emissions (0.44 kg CO2e/kg) come from the Carbon Trust–certified footprint of a Diet Coke can (150 g CO2e, GB 2009). Diet Coke is the same drink without sugar, so this covers everything except the sugar crop. A glass bottle has more than double the footprint of a can. Factory water is Coca-Cola's reported 1.78 L per L of drink.

Vitamins and minerals come from a stand-in USDA record (generic regular cola) because the label doesn't list them.

source.title: Coca-Cola US — Coca-Cola Original nutrition facts and ingredients
source.note: Coca-Cola — nutrition per gram: 140 kcal, 39 g sugar (= carbs), 45 mg sodium, 0 fat/protein per can ÷ 369 g. Label per 355 mL can × ~1.04 g/mL (a ~10.5% sugar solution) = 369 g per can. USDA generic regular cola (SR 14148, FDC 174852) is similar: 42 kcal, 9.94 g sugar, 3 mg sodium per 100 g.

name: Coke Zero (Composite)
notes:
Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, modelled from its ingredients. It has no sugar: it's carbonated water, caramel colour, phosphoric acid, flavours, caffeine and the sweeteners aspartame and acesulfame potassium. It has no modelled crop footprint (no land, pesticides or farm emissions). The sweeteners aren't added as ingredients because: acesulfame potassium is made from petroleum-based chemicals, not a crop; aspartame is made by fermenting sugar or corn, but a can has only ~0.1–0.2 g of sweetener in 355 g, so the footprint would barely change; and adding them would wrongly make Coke Zero look scarce, because availability averages the ingredients' world supply (only tens of Gg for these sweeteners) rather than how much drink that supply could make.

Nutrition is from Coke's own label: zero calories, a little sodium and potassium.

Factory, can, distribution, chilling and disposal emissions (0.45 kg CO2e/kg) come from the Carbon Trust–certified footprint of a Diet Coke / Coke Zero can (150 g CO2e, GB 2009). A glass bottle has more than double the footprint of a can. Factory water is Coca-Cola's reported 1.78 L per L of drink.

Vitamins and minerals not on the label are a guess copied from USDA's generic regular cola, which has the same base.

Availability is copied from the Coca-Cola entry. With no crop ingredients the math has no base to work from, so Coke's number is used. In theory it could be far higher, since a little sweetener makes a lot of drink.
